# Coordinated dilation: exact obstruction fibers, asymptotics, and partition failure

Let `C` be a compact convex body in `R^n x R^d`. Write `K_z=C_z` for its
integer fibers and let finitely many open caps

    U_i={(z,x):u_i dot z+v_i dot x>b_i}

cover the mixed set `S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d)`. Their complementary
closed polyhedron is

    P={(z,x):u_i dot z+v_i dot x<=b_i for every i}.

The hypothesis is `C intersect P intersect (Z^n x R^d)=empty`.
It does **not** say that `P` itself is mixed-integer-free. In particular,
its integer fibers `Q_z=P_z` can be nonempty outside `K_z`.

Let `c(z)=Az+a` be any affine continuous-coordinate map. It need not be
an actual selector unless explicitly required. For `s>=1` set

    C_s={(z,c(z)+s(x-c(z))):(z,x) in C}.

This is an invertible affine image of `C`. It is convex and compact,
has exactly the same integer projection, and has fibers
`K_z(s)=c(z)+s(K_z-c(z))`. The map preserves the mixed lattice because
the integer coordinate is unchanged. An **interior selector** means
`c(z) in int(K_z)` at every relevant full-dimensional fiber; a selector
without that adjective means membership in `K_z`.

## 1. Exact classification for every compact convex fiber

For a nonempty compact convex set `K` and a point `c`, define

    cone(K-c)={t(x-c):t>=0,x in K}.

Convexity of `K-c` makes this an ordinary convex cone; closure is not
included in its definition. Then

    union_{s>=1} [c+s(K-c)] = K+cone(K-c).           (1)

Indeed `c+s(x-c)=x+(s-1)(x-c)` gives one inclusion. Conversely,
`x+t(y-c)=c+(1+t)(k-c)` with `k=(x+t y)/(1+t) in K`, giving the other.
Consequently the fixed open cap cover persists for every `s>=1` if and
only if

    [K_z+cone(K_z-c(z))] intersect Q_z=empty        (2)

at every nonempty integer fiber. This condition includes lower-dimensional
and zero-measure fibers, which still matter for coverage. An empty `Q_z`
never obstructs dilation. If every relevant `Q_z` is empty, every affine
map `c` is admissible for indefinite coverage.

If `K_z` is full-dimensional and `c(z)` is interior, the union in (1)
is all of `R^d`: an interior ball about the center expands to arbitrary
radius. If all nonempty fibers are full-dimensional, an interior selector
therefore permits indefinite coverage exactly when `Q_z=empty` at
**every** relevant integer fiber. Any nonempty `Q_z` in such a fiber is
met at a finite dilation parameter. Lower-dimensional fibers must also
be checked when present. There a relative-interior center instead fills
the fiber's affine hull; the corresponding obstruction is intersection
of `Q_z` with that affine hull.

## 2. Exact separating-hyperplane criterion for polytopal fibers

Suppose `K` is a nonempty polytope, `Q` a nonempty polyhedron, and
`K intersect Q=empty`. Write `h_K(beta)=max_{x in K} beta dot x`.
Then (2) for this pair is equivalent to the existence of `beta!=0` with

    beta dot c>=h_K(beta),
    inf_{q in Q} beta dot q>h_K(beta).              (3)

Sufficiency is immediate: every dilated point has scalar product at most

    s h_K(beta)+(1-s) beta dot c<=h_K(beta),

so it stays strictly separated from `Q`.

For necessity, write `K={Bx<=d}` and `Q={Ex<=f}`. The intersection in
(2) is nonempty precisely when the following linear system in `x,s` is
feasible:

    Ex<=f,
    Bx-s(d-Bc)<=Bc,
    -s<=-1.

Indeed the middle inequalities say `c+(x-c)/s in K`. If the system is
infeasible, the finite-dimensional Farkas lemma gives multipliers
`lambda>=0,eta>=0,theta>=0` such that

    lambda E+eta B=0,
    eta(Bc-d)=theta>=0,
    lambda f+eta Bc-theta=lambda f+eta d<0.

Put `beta=eta B=-lambda E`. On `K`, `beta dot x<=eta d`, while
`beta dot c=eta Bc>=eta d`. On `Q`, `beta dot q>=-lambda f>eta d`.
Thus (3) follows. The vector `beta` cannot be zero because then the two
displayed bounds would contradict nonemptiness of both `K` and `Q`.
This proof does not require full-dimensional fibers.

For a genuine selector `c in K`, the first inequality in (3) is equality:
the center must belong to a supporting face pointing towards `Q`.
Exterior centers have more freedom: placing the center past that face,
towards `Q`, can make the separation persist indefinitely.

The polytope qualification in (3) is essential. Let `K` be the closed
unit disk centered at `(1,0)`, let `c=(0,0)`, and let `Q={(0,1)}`. Every
dilate is the disk centered at `(s,0)` of radius `s`, so it misses `Q`
for every finite `s`. Its union is `{(x,y):x>0} union {(0,0)}` and is
not closed. But `h_K(beta)=beta_x+|beta|<=beta dot c=0` forces
`beta=(-a,0)` with `a>0`; on `Q` this gives zero, equal to `h_K(beta)`.
No strict separator (3) exists. The exact union criterion (2), without
closing the cone, remains valid for arbitrary compact convex fibers.

## 3. Exact cap asymptotics and boundary mass

Put `q=dim_H S`, and measure `S` intrinsically by `H_q`. At each fiber
the continuous-coordinate dilation scales its `q`-measure by `s^q`;
lower-dimensional fibers have zero `H_q`-mass when `q>0`. The finite
fiber-sum identity therefore gives

    H_q(S_s)=s^q H_q(S).                            (4)

This also holds for `q=0`, with counting measure. Let `M=H_q(S)>0`,
and, on the original fiber, put

    r_{i,z}(x)=v_i dot(x-c(z)),
    delta_{i,z}=b_i-u_i dot z-v_i dot c(z).

For the corresponding closed cap `H_i`, its normalized mass after
dilation is exactly

    p_i(s)=M^{-1} sum_z H_q{
       x in K_z:r_{i,z}(x)>=delta_{i,z}/s}.          (5)

Pointwise indicator convergence, followed by dominated convergence over
the finite fiber sum, gives

    lim_{s->infinity} p_i(s)
      =M^{-1} sum_z [
          H_q{x in K_z:r_{i,z}(x)>0}
          +1_{delta_{i,z}<=0} H_q{x in K_z:r_{i,z}(x)=0}]. (6)

The boundary term is necessary: it cannot always be replaced by the
mass of the closed limiting halfspace. For positive full-dimensional
`d`-fibers and `v_i!=0`, this term vanishes, and the simpler expression is

    M^{-1} sum_z vol_d{
       x in K_z:v_i dot(x-c(z))>=0}.                (7)

For vertical caps `v_i=0`, formula (6) instead retains exactly the
unchanged integer-coordinate inequality. In particular, the integer
part of an oblique cap disappears from (7) except through the chosen
affine field `c(z)`, while it still determines whether the cap cover can
survive through all finite parameters. Neither mass convergence nor a
favorable limiting mass alone establishes condition (2).

## 4. What positive continuous circuits actually identify

Write the fiber inequalities of `P` as

    v_i dot x<=b_i-u_i dot z.

The Farkas lemma gives the exact criterion

    Q_z=empty iff there is lambda>=0 with
      sum_i lambda_i v_i=0 and
      sum_i lambda_i(b_i-u_i dot z)<0.              (8)

Normalize nonzero multipliers by `sum lambda_i=1`. The resulting set is
a compact polytope. Its extreme points have at most `d+1` nonzero
coordinates (or the rank of the continuous normals plus one). Indeed,
with a larger support the continuous-normal equations together with the
normalization equation have a nonzero kernel vector on that support;
small perturbations in both signs preserve nonnegativity and all the
equations, contradicting extremality. Thus it
suffices in (8) to check the finite set of positive circuits. Equivalently,
the projection of `P` is the polyhedron on which every circuit's common
affine term is nonnegative.

This criterion detects fibers where dilation is automatically harmless.
It does not select supporting centers at the nonempty fibers. Even a
single constant positive circuit term can coexist with incompatible
supporting-center requirements at many integer indices, as the next
example shows. Therefore circuit signs alone are not an allocation or
volume-budget theorem.

## 5. A minimal equal-cap cover requiring more than 2^n selector regions

Here `n=d=1`. For `0<=z<=9` let `g(z)` be the piecewise affine convex
interpolant of `g(j)=j^2` at integers `j=0,...,9`, and set `L=257/2`.
Equivalently,

    g(z)=max_{j=0,...,8}[(2j+1)z-j(j+1)].

Define the full-dimensional convex polygon

    C={(z,x):0<=z<=9, g(z)<=x<=L}.

Its ten integer fibers are `[j^2,L]`, all with positive length. Their
total mass is

    M=10L-sum_{j=0}^9 j^2=1285-285=1000.

Let `p(z)=130z-382` and take the two open caps with closed versions

    U_+={x-p(z)>1/2}, H_+={x-p(z)>=1/2},
    U_-={x-p(z)<-1/2}, H_-={x-p(z)<=-1/2}.

Their complementary polyhedron is the strip

    P={|x-p(z)|<=1/2}.

At indices `0,...,3`, its entire fiber lies strictly below `C_j`; the
closest case is `j=3`, where the strip is `[15/2,17/2]` and `C_3`
starts at nine. At indices `4,...,9`, its fiber lies strictly above
`C_j`; the closest case is `j=4`, where the strip starts at `275/2>L`.
Hence the two open caps strictly cover `S`. They are inclusion-minimal,
with strict interior witnesses in the two respective groups of fibers.
Their masses are equal:

    sum_{j=0}^3 (L-j^2)=4L-14=500,
    sum_{j=4}^9 (L-j^2)=6L-271=500.

Each normalized cap mass is `1/2`. No fiber carries half the total mass;
the largest has mass `257/2000`. The example concerns the proposed
decomposition mechanism; its cap threshold is not below the OC bound.

For an interval `K=[a,b]` and a nonempty interval `Q` strictly below it,
indefinite dilation about a point `c in K` is possible only when `c=a`:
if `c>a`, the lower endpoint `c+s(a-c)` moves to minus infinity and
crosses `Q` at a finite parameter. Conversely `c=a` keeps the dilate
above `Q`. Similarly, when `Q` is above `K`, a selector center must
equal `b`. Thus every admissible selector in this example must satisfy

    c(j)=j^2, j=0,1,2,3;
    c(j)=L,   j=4,5,6,7,8,9.                       (9)

There is no partition of these ten integer indices into at most two
regions, even arbitrary nonconvex regions, such that an affine selector
on each region satisfies (9). Every affine function agrees with `j^2`
at at most two distinct indices among `0,1,2,3`. To cover those four
indices with two affine functions, each must therefore agree at exactly
two. The secant through `(a,a^2),(b,b^2)`, with `0<=a<b<=3`, is

    c(z)=(a+b)z-ab.

For `4<=z<=9`, its value is at most `5z-6<=39<L`. Neither function can
serve any index from the right group. This contradicts the proposed
two-region partition. Hence more than `2^n=2` affine **selector**
regions are necessary, even for a minimal strict equal-cap cover with
nonheavy fibers.

Exterior affine centers behave differently: the single affine map
`c(z)=p(z)` lies in the middle of every obstructing strip fiber. It is
below `K_j` for `j<=3` and above it for `j>=4`, so all corresponding
dilates move away from the strip. It preserves this cap cover for every
`s>=1`. Thus the example does not refute a statement allowing exterior
centers, and those centers must not be silently called selectors.

The only positive continuous circuit of these two opposite cap normals
has equal multipliers. Its common term is the constant width of the
strip, positive at every `z`. There are no circuit-sign transition
hyperplanes that detect the changes in (9). This explicitly separates
the circuit test for empty `P_z` from the geometry needed for supporting
center selection.

## 6. Exterior affine centers can also be globally incompatible

The successful exterior map in the preceding example is not a general
existence theorem. For an exact obstruction, take `n=2,d=1` and

    C=[0,1]^2 x [0,1].

Let `P` be the tetrahedron with vertices

    (0,0,-1), (1,0,2), (0,1,2), (1,1,-1).

Its barycentric coordinates are

    lambda_0=(5-3z_1-3z_2-x)/6,
    lambda_1=(3z_1-3z_2+x+1)/6,
    lambda_2=(-3z_1+3z_2+x+1)/6,
    lambda_3=(3z_1+3z_2-x-1)/6.

Their sum is one, and direct substitution gives the unit coordinate
vectors at the four specified vertices, so `P={all lambda_i>=0}`.
The four open caps `U_i={lambda_i<0}` have closed versions
`H_i={lambda_i<=0}`. On each integer fiber of `C` exactly one of them
contains the entire interval strictly, and all others miss it:

    (0,0): cap 3; (1,0): cap 2;
    (0,1): cap 1; (1,1): cap 0.

Thus this is a minimal strict equal-mass cover, each cap mass `1/4`.
The four integer fibers of `P` are singletons: `-1` at the two diagonal
indices and `2` at the two off-diagonal indices. They miss the original
fiber `[0,1]`.

For dilation of `[0,1]` about an arbitrary real point `c` to avoid the
point `-1` forever, one must have `c<=0`. If `c>0`, its lower endpoint
`c-sc` eventually crosses `-1`, while its upper endpoint is larger by
`s`, so the dilate meets that point at a finite parameter. Conversely
`c<=0` keeps the whole dilate above it. Similarly, avoiding the point
`2` forever is equivalent to `c>=1`. Therefore a globally admissible
affine map would require

    c(0,0)<=0, c(1,1)<=0,
    c(1,0)>=1, c(0,1)>=1.

But every affine map on the square satisfies

    c(0,0)+c(1,1)=c(1,0)+c(0,1),

contradicting these inequalities. Hence no affine center map, even one
allowed to lie outside all fibers, preserves this cap cover for every
`s>=1`. This is an obstruction to global compatibility, not to the
per-fiber separating criterion (3).

## 7. Volume accounting does not automatically glue regions

For a disjoint partition of the finite integer indices into `J_r`, let
`M_r=sum_{z in J_r} H_q(K_z)`. Then `sum_r M_r=M` exactly. Dilating the
fibers of each region by a factor `s_r` gives intrinsic mass

    sum_r s_r^q M_r

for that disjoint union of fibers. Equal factors give `s^q M`. These are
valid identities before any convexification. Different affine center
maps on different regions need not combine into a single affine map or
even a convex inducing body. Taking their convex hull can enlarge
intermediate integer fibers, change cap masses, and destroy the cap
cover. A piecewise dilation argument therefore needs an additional proved
gluing mechanism; the budget identities alone do not supply one.

The exact arithmetic of the counterexample is checked by
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_coordinated_dilation_classification.py`. No minimizer existence,
monotonicity of asymptotic cap masses, or general circuit allocation is
assumed here.
